title: Chapter 94 — A Squeeze of the Hand
paragraphs: Stubb's whale, bought at such a high price, was brought alongside the Pequod in due course, and all the cutting and hoisting operations described earlier were carried out in the usual way, right down to bailing out the Heidelburgh Tun, or Case.

While some were occupied with this latter duty, others were employed in dragging away the larger tubs as soon as they were filled with sperm. And when the proper time arrived, this same sperm was carefully processed before going to the try-works, of which more later.

The sperm had cooled and crystallized so much that when I sat down with several others in front of a large Constantine's bath of it, I found it had oddly set into lumps, which rolled about here and there in the liquid. Our job was to squeeze these lumps back into fluid. A sweet, oily duty! No wonder this sperm was such a popular cosmetic in the old days. What a cleanser! What a sweetener! What a softener! What a delicious soother! After my hands had been in it just a few minutes, my fingers felt like eels and began, so to speak, to snake and spiral.

As I sat there at my ease, cross-legged on the deck — after the bitter exertion at the windlass, under a blue tranquil sky, the ship under lazy sail and gliding so serenely along — as I bathed my hands among those soft, gentle globules of infiltrated tissue, woven almost within the hour, as they richly broke to my fingers and discharged all their richness, like fully ripe grapes their wine, as I breathed in that uncontaminated aroma, literally and truly like the smell of spring violets — I declare to you that for the time I lived as in a musky meadow. I forgot all about our horrible oath. In that inexpressible sperm, I washed my hands and my heart of it. I almost began to credit the old Paracelsan superstition that sperm is of rare virtue in calming the heat of anger. While bathing in that bath, I felt divinely free from all ill-will, or irritation, or malice of any sort whatsoever.

Squeeze! Squeeze! Squeeze! All the morning long I squeezed that sperm till I myself almost melted into it. I squeezed that sperm till a strange sort of madness came over me, and I found myself unwittingly squeezing my co-workers' hands in it, mistaking their hands for the gentle globules. Such an overflowing, affectionate, friendly, loving feeling did this work beget that at last I was continually squeezing their hands and looking up into their eyes sentimentally — as much as to say: Oh, my dear fellow beings, why should we any longer harbor any social bitterness, or know the slightest ill-humor or envy! Come, let us squeeze hands all round. No, let us all squeeze ourselves into each other. Let us squeeze ourselves universally into the very milk and sperm of kindness.

If only I could go on squeezing that sperm forever! Long, repeated experience has taught me that in every case a man must eventually lower, or at least relocate, his notion of the happiness he can reach — placing it not in the intellect or the imagination at all, but in the wife, the heart, the bed, the table, the saddle, the fireside, the country. Now that I have seen all this, I am ready to squeeze case for all eternity. In thoughts of the visions of the night, I saw long rows of angels in paradise, each with his hands in a jar of spermaceti.
Now, while speaking of sperm, it is fitting to mention other things related to it in the business of preparing the sperm whale for the try-works.

First there is what is called white-horse, which comes from the tapering part of the fish and from the thicker parts of his flukes. It is tough with congealed tendons — a wad of muscle — but it still holds some oil. Once it has been cut from the whale, the white-horse is first chopped into oblong pieces small enough to carry, before it goes to the mincer. These look a lot like blocks of Berkshire marble.

Plum-pudding is the name given to certain scraps of the whale's flesh that stick here and there to the blanket of blubber and often share a good deal of its oiliness. It is a most refreshing, festive, beautiful thing to look at. As the name suggests, it has an extremely rich, mottled color: a streaky snow-white and golden ground dotted with spots of the deepest crimson and purple. It is plums of ruby set in pictures of citron. Against all reason, it is hard to stop yourself from eating it. I admit that I once slipped behind the foremast to taste some. It tasted rather as I imagine a royal cutlet from the thigh of Louis le Gros might have tasted — supposing he had been killed on the first day after the venison season, and that this particular venison season had coincided with an unusually fine vintage in the vineyards of Champagne.

There is another substance, a very singular one, which turns up in the course of this business, but which I find very difficult to adequately describe. It is called slobgollion — a name original with the whalemen, and the substance itself is just as original. It is an indescribably oozy, stringy affair, most frequently found in the tubs of sperm after a prolonged squeezing and subsequent decanting. I hold it to be the wondrously thin, ruptured membranes of the case, fused together.

Gurry, as it is called, is strictly a right whalemen's term, though the sperm whalers sometimes use it in passing. It means the dark, sticky substance scraped off the back of the Greenland or right whale, and a great deal of it ends up covering the decks of those inferior souls who hunt that ignoble Leviathan.

Nippers. Strictly, this word is not native to the whale's vocabulary. But as applied by whalemen, it becomes so. A whaleman's nipper is a short, firm strip of tendinous stuff cut from the tapering part of Leviathan's tail. It averages an inch in thickness and is otherwise about the size of the iron part of a hoe. Moved edgewise along the oily deck, it works like a leather squeegee, and by nameless coaxings, as if by magic, it lures along with it all impurities.

But to learn all about these obscure matters, your best course is to go straight down into the blubber-room and have a long talk with its inmates. This place has previously been mentioned as the receptacle for the blanket-pieces when stripped and hoisted from the whale. When the time comes to cut up its contents, this room becomes a scene of terror to all newcomers, especially at night. On one side, lit by a dull lantern, a space has been cleared for the workmen. They generally go in pairs — a pike-and-gaff man and a spademan. The whaling-pike is similar to a frigate's boarding-weapon of the same name. The gaff is something like a boat-hook. With his gaff, the gaffman hooks onto a sheet of blubber and tries to hold it from slipping as the ship pitches and lurches about. Meanwhile, the spademan stands on the sheet itself, chopping it perpendicularly into portable horse-pieces. This spade is as sharp as a whetstone can make it. The spademan's feet are shoeless. The thing he stands on will sometimes irresistibly slide away from him like a sled. If he cuts off one of his own toes, or one of his assistants', would you be very much surprised? Toes are scarce among veteran blubber-room men.
